opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's one of the most fundamental challenges any intelligent creature has ever had to solve. If you go back about 540 million years, to the Cambrian period, that's when animals first developed eyes, and many evolutionary biologists believe that's what triggered the Cambrian explosion. Suddenly, organisms could see the world around them, and the moment you can see, you have to make sense of what you're seeing. Where is the food? Where is the predator? How far away is it? How do I move toward it or away from it? That loop between perceiving and acting in a three-dimensional world is really the origin of intelligence as we know it.

So for me, spatial intelligence isn't just one capability among many. It's the scaffolding that much of the rest is built on. Language came very late in evolution, only a few hundred thousand years ago for humans. But the ability to understand the 3D structure of the world, to reason about objects, their relationships, their physics, and to interact with them, took hundreds of millions of years to evolve. Nature spent an enormous amount of time on this problem, and that tells you something about how hard it is.

And it's hard partly because the world is 3D, but what we receive through our eyes is essentially a 2D projection. The brain has to reconstruct and infer the depth, the geometry, the occlusions, the dynamics, and do it in real time. A squirrel jumping between branches, a child stacking blocks, a surgeon operating, a builder framing a house: all of these depend on a rich internal model of space and how things move and change within it.

Humans take it further. We don't just navigate space, we create in it. We build cities, design tools, make art, and we can imagine spaces that don't exist yet. That generative side of spatial intelligence is incredibly powerful, and it's a big part of why I'm so excited about bringing this capability to AI. Language models have made remarkable progress, but language is a lossy, one-dimensional signal about a world that is fundamentally three-dimensional and physical. If we want machines that can truly understand, reason about, and act in the real world, alongside us, they need spatial intelligence.

r002.rationale: It describes spatial intelligence as difficult and says nature spent hundreds of millions of years on it, but does not state that evolution has only partially solved it in animals.

r003.rationale: It says humans create and imagine spaces, but does not say people generally struggle to generate complex 3D models of their surroundings without training.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. You know, I always start with the evolutionary story, because I think it tells us something fundamental.

If you look back about 540 million years, to the Cambrian explosion, one of the very first things that happens is that animals develop the ability to sense light. The first eyes, if you can even call them that, were just light-sensitive patches. But the moment an animal could perceive the world around it, everything changed. It could find food. It could avoid becoming food. It could move with purpose. And that perception created pressure on the nervous system to understand what it was seeing, to represent where things are, how they're moving, how to act on them. So perception and action and intelligence co-evolved together. Vision didn't just come along for the ride. In many ways it was the trigger.

And here's what I find really striking. For animals, including us, spatial intelligence is not a nice-to-have. It is the foundation. Long before there was language, long before there were symbols or abstract reasoning, there was an animal that needed to know: where am I, what is around me, how do I get from here to there, how do I reach out and grasp that thing. Every creature that moves has had to solve this. A bee navigating back to its hive, a bird landing on a branch in the wind, a cat judging a jump. These are extraordinarily hard computational problems, and nature solved them over hundreds of millions of years.

For humans, it's just as deep. A baby, before it can say a single word, is building a model of the physical world. It understands object permanence, that things persist when they go behind the couch. It understands that if you tilt a cup the water comes out. It's reaching, grabbing, failing, trying again. Our spatial understanding is so effortless to us that we don't even notice it. We walk into a room and we instantly know its layout, we know which chair to sit in, we know not to bump into the table. It feels trivial. But that effortlessness is exactly the sign of how deeply it's been optimized in us, and how hard the underlying problem actually is.

So when I think about spatial intelligence as a challenge, I think it's humbling. Language is a relatively recent invention, maybe a few hundred thousand years old. Spatial intelligence is half a billion years old. It is how we perceive, how we reason about the physical world, how we imagine, how we create, how we interact. If we want to build machines that are truly intelligent, that can be in the world and act in it alongside us, I believe we have to take this challenge as seriously as nature did.

r002.rationale: It describes spatial intelligence as difficult and says nature solved these problems over hundreds of millions of years; it does not say evolution has only partially solved them.

r003.rationale: It describes humans’ effortless everyday spatial understanding and babies building a model of the physical world, but does not state that humans generally struggle to generate complex three-dimensional models without training.

astra-6.text:
I think spatial intelligence is one of the most fundamental forms of intelligence. For an animal, including a human, the world is not just something you look at. It’s something you have to act in. You have to understand where things are, how they relate to one another, what’s moving, and what might happen when you move.

Think about a cat jumping from the floor onto a counter. It’s doing something quite remarkable: relating its own body to the geometry of the world and turning that understanding into an action. We do this all the time, too. When you reach for a cup, you’re judging distance, anticipating contact, and adjusting your movement as you go. It feels effortless, but there’s an enormous amount of intelligence in that loop between perception and action.

So spatial intelligence is much more than recognizing objects in an image. It’s understanding a three-dimensional, changing world well enough to interact with it. And that’s a foundational challenge for animals because their survival depends on it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think spatial intelligence is one of the most fundamental forms of intelligence, and it’s something we take for granted. For animals, including humans, the world is three-dimensional. We move through it, we interact with objects, we navigate around obstacles. Even something as simple as reaching for a cup requires you to understand where it is, its shape, how your hand should approach it, and what will happen when you touch it.

So this is much more than recognizing what’s in an image. It’s understanding the relationships between things, anticipating how they might change, and knowing how your own actions can affect them. Perception and action are deeply connected.

And evolution has been working on this for a very long time. A lot of that intelligence happens without language or conscious deliberation. We don’t solve equations every time we walk across a room. But underneath that apparently effortless behavior is an extraordinary ability to understand and interact with the physical world.
